title: Search the Answer
focus: Week three. Binary search stops being about arrays, design gets its O(1) randomness, and DP grows a state machine.

cards.title: Binary Search on the Answer
patterns: Search the value range, not the index range
cards.trigger: Minimise the maximum, or maximise the minimum, and you can check a candidate answer in linear time.
cards.recall: Write the Koko solution from memory. Then answer the question that unlocks the whole family: what makes the predicate monotonic here, and how do you prove your search space bounds are correct?
useWhen: Minimum eating speed, minimum ship capacity, minimum days
Split an array into k parts minimising the largest part
Maximum minimum distance, magnetic force between balls
Kth smallest in a sorted matrix, by counting elements at most x
Any 'minimise the maximum' or 'maximise the minimum' phrasing
template: # 1. Identify the answer range [lo, hi] and prove both ends are safe.
# 2. Write feasible(x): can we do it with x? It must be monotonic in x.
# 3. Binary search the smallest feasible x.
return sum(math.ceil(p / speed) for p in piles) <= h
lo, hi = 1, max(piles)      # 1 is always slow enough to be infeasible-or-not
while lo < hi:              # find the FIRST feasible speed
keyInsights: Monotonic means: if speed x works, every speed above x works. State that explicitly, it is the correctness argument
The search space is the range of possible ANSWERS, not indices. That reframing is the entire trick
It is the same boundary template from Day 3. If that one is solid, this is a new `feasible` function and nothing else
cards.trap: 'What is the complexity?' It is O(n log(range)), not O(log n). The feasibility check is linear and runs on every step. Getting that wrong reads as not understanding your own solution.

cards.title: O(1) Insert, Delete, Random
patterns: Swap with the last, then pop
cards.trigger: You need uniform random selection alongside O(1) insert and delete.
cards.recall: Sketch the two structures from memory. Then write `remove`, and answer: why swap with the last element instead of deleting in place, and what index bookkeeping must accompany the swap?
useWhen: Insert, delete and get-random all in O(1)
Random pick with weights, that one wants prefix sums plus binary search
Reservoir sampling over a stream
Shuffle an array, Fisher-Yates
Any structure needing both membership and uniform sampling
template: self.arr = []        # dense array -> O(1) random index
self.pos = {}        # value -> its index in arr
if val in self.pos: return False
if val not in self.pos: return False
self.arr[i] = last          # move the last element into the hole
self.pos[last] = i          # and fix ITS recorded index
del self.pos[val]           # delete after, order matters when val is last
keyInsights: Random access needs a dense array. Deleting from the middle of an array is O(n) unless you swap with the last
Updating `pos[last]` is the line people forget, and the bug only shows after two removes
Deleting `val` from the map after the swap handles the case where val was itself the last element
cards.trap: 'Now allow duplicates.' The map must hold a SET of indices per value, and remove becomes trickier. Know that the shape changes.

cards.title: Subtree and Structural Match
patterns: Try every node as a root
cards.trigger: Does one tree appear inside another, or are two trees identical.
cards.recall: Write `is_same` and `is_subtree` from memory. Then answer: what is the naive complexity, and how does the serialize-and-search approach get to linear?
useWhen: Subtree of another tree, same tree, symmetric tree
Find duplicate subtrees
Merge two binary trees
Leaf-similar trees
Any structural comparison of two trees
template: if not a and not b: return True
if not a or not b:  return False           # one None, one not
return is_subtree(root.left, sub) or is_subtree(root.right, sub)
# Linear alternative: serialize both with null markers and unique delimiters,
# then ask whether sub's string is a substring of root's string.
#   '#4#5' would falsely match inside '#14#5', so pad: f',{val},'
# Symmetric tree: is_mirror(a.left, b.right) and is_mirror(a.right, b.left)

complexity.time: O(m * n) naive, O(m + n) serialized

keyInsights: The two None checks must be in that order. Checking `a.val` before proving both exist is the crash
Serialising to a string turns tree matching into string matching, so KMP gives you linear. Mention it even if you write the simple one
Delimiters matter. Without padding, value 4 matches inside value 14 and you report a false subtree
cards.trap: 'Duplicate subtrees, return one root per distinct duplicate.' Serialize every subtree into a counter map. The naive pairwise comparison is quadratic and they will time you out.

cards.title: State Machine DP
cards.trigger: You are in one of a few modes at each step, and each mode has its own best value.
cards.recall: Draw the three states and the arrows between them before revealing. Then write the transitions. If you can draw the machine you cannot get the code wrong.
useWhen: Stock buy and sell, with cooldown, with fees, with at most k transactions
Paint house, paint fence, any per-step categorical choice
Alternating or parity constrained sequences
Regex or automaton style matching
Any DP where the natural state is a mode rather than a number
template: # Three states, and what each MEANS at the end of day i:
#   hold  = best profit while holding a share
#   sold  = best profit having just sold today (cooldown applies tomorrow)
#   rest  = best profit holding nothing and free to buy
hold, sold, rest = (max(hold, rest - p),   # keep holding, or buy from rest
hold + p,             # sell what we held
max(rest, sold))      # stay free, or cool down from sold
# k transactions: two arrays of size k+1

problem.name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown

keyInsights: The simultaneous tuple assignment is what keeps all three transitions reading yesterday's values. Sequential assignment silently uses today's
Cooldown is not a new algorithm, it is one extra state. Say that when they add the constraint
Naming states in English before coding is the same discipline as the state sentence in ordinary DP
cards.trap: 'Now k can be as large as the number of days.' Above n/2 transactions the constraint is meaningless and it collapses to the unlimited case. Spotting that saves you from a quadratic table.

cards.title: Permutation Backtracking
cards.trigger: Order matters and every element must appear exactly once.
cards.recall: Write permutations from memory, both the used-array version and the swap version. Then answer: for permutations with duplicates, why is the skip condition `not used[i-1]` and not `used[i-1]`?
useWhen: All permutations, with or without duplicates
Letter case permutation, phone letter combinations
Assignment problems over a small n
Sequence reconstruction under constraints
Any 'all orderings' phrasing with n at most about 10
template: # With duplicates: sort, then skip an equal element whose twin is NOT in use
if used[i] or (i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1] and not used[i-1]):
# In-place swap variant: O(1) extra space beyond the output
keyInsights: `not used[i-1]` forces duplicates to be consumed left to right, so each multiset ordering is generated exactly once
The swap version does not preserve sorted order during recursion, so the duplicate skip does not work with it. Pick one
n! at n = 10 is 3.6 million. Above that, backtracking is not the intended solution and you should say so
cards.trap: 'Why is it n * n! and not n!?' Because copying each permutation into the output is O(n). Same reason subsets is n * 2^n.
